revisions.text: Anhua tea is kept for years and said to improve: the liquor turns redder and the taste sweeter and mellower, with a fuller scent. No agreed count of years marks it as aged. Keep it clean, dry and aired, away from mould and other smells.
In a small pot or gaiwan, use water at the boil and start with a steep of about 15 to 30 seconds, a little longer each round. Pressed and aged Anhua tea is also commonly simmered in a pot.

Pine smoke or pine resin above all, a sweet taste and aftertaste, and a mellow, thick, smooth cup; a liquor from yellow and orange to orange-red. Young tea is often smokier in the first infusions and a little bitter, sweetening as the infusions go on.

Anhua dark tea comes from Anhua County, a mountain county on the Zi river in north-central Hunan, under the city of Yiyang. Its name is a protected origin product in China, so it is tied to a defined place of making. Anhua is widely named as the main home of dark tea in China, and as a starting point of the old tea routes to the north-west.

Anhua teas come in three shapes. The three tips are loose teas, lightly pressed into bamboo baskets: Tianjian from the most tender leaf, Gongjian in the middle, and Shengjian, the coarsest, with the most stalk. The pressed bricks are Fu, Hei and Hua brick; Fu brick is the one grown on purpose with golden flower, in a warm, humid room for some weeks before it is dried hard. The flower rolls are tall columns pressed by hand inside a woven bamboo basket lined with leaf, named by their old weight in liang: Qianliang, a thousand, Bailiang, a hundred, and Shiliang, ten. Huajuan, flower roll, names the whole family and is also a nickname of Qianliang.
The raw leaf is sorted into numbered grades, and each finished tea is made from the grade that suits it, the most tender leaf going into the finest loose tips.

Anhua became a county in 1072, in the Northern Song, and tea from the area is mentioned from the Tang on, though as tea from the place, not yet as dark tea. In 1595, in the Ming, Anhua tea became an official tea, sold to the north-west. In the Qing, Shanxi merchants and others took over the border trade, and the loose tips and the large rolls grew out of that trade; the rolls are a Qing product, not a Ming one. Fu brick was first made in Anhua itself in 1953, at the Baishaxi factory, after Fu bricks had long been pressed in Shaanxi from Anhua raw tea.

Every Anhua tea starts as one raw tea, heimaocha, made from large Anhua leaf. The leaf is fixed, rolled, piled, rolled again and dried over a wood fire, and in Anhua that fire burns pine. The pine fire gives the tea its smell of pine smoke or pine resin, which sets it apart from dark teas dried another way; some newer lines dry by machine instead. The raw tea is then steamed soft and pressed: lightly for the loose tips, in moulds for the bricks, and by hand for the rolls.
A redder liquor, a sweeter, mellower cup, and sometimes a medicinal or herbal note.

A roll is packed into its basket and pressed tight by treading and twisting with long bars, then left to dry slowly in sun and night air for weeks rather than in a dryer. Rolls are usually kept whole to age, and reach drinkers later as slices, discs or small cut pieces, since a whole roll is far too big to buy or brew.
Freshly roasted Dancong is rested for some months before it is at its best; how many months is not agreed. Keep it sealed, dry, cool and out of the light.

Dancong is sorted and sold by its aroma type, named for a flower, fruit or spice the scent recalls. The scent comes from the bush and the making, not from anything added: an orchid or almond Dancong names a smell, not an ingredient. The trade speaks of the ten aroma types. Nine names turn up in every full list: Huangzhi, yellow sprig; Zhilan, orchid; Milan, honey orchid; Yulan, magnolia; Xingren, almond; Jianghua, ginger flower; Guihua, osmanthus; Yelai, night-blooming flower; and Rougui, cinnamon. The tenth is most often jasmine.

Brew it gongfu style in a small gaiwan or clay pot, with about 3 to 8 grams for 100 to 120 ml and hot water, about 88 to 100°C; Chinese accounts mostly say 95 to 100°C. A quick rinse is common. Steeps start at a few seconds and grow a few seconds each round, and a good Dancong gives about eight to fifteen. Too long, too hot or too much leaf and it turns bitter and astringent.

Flowers above all, a sweetness that comes back after swallowing, a high scent that lasts, honey, often ripe fruit such as peach, and what the trade calls mountain rhyme, shan yun; a liquor from golden to orange-red or amber.

Phoenix Dancong is the oolong of Phoenix Mountain, Fenghuang Shan, in Chao'an, Chaozhou, in eastern Guangdong. Wudong is the peak named most often as its heart. The dry leaf is a long strip, twisted tight, dark and glossy, not rolled into a ball.

The old tea of the mountain was called bird-beak tea, and later Shuixian. Dancong is the everyday tea of Chaozhou, and gongfu brewing is tied to Chaozhou, where Chaozhou gongfu tea is still made with small vessels, set ways of pouring, and three cups.

The leaf is withered in the sun and cooled indoors, then shaken and rested in rounds; this is the step that bruises the leaf edge and builds the scent. It is fixed fast at high heat in a hot pan or drum, rolled into strips, dried, and roasted again as it is refined, sometimes over more than one round. Charcoal is the traditional fire. The roast is a main difference between teas: a light roast keeps the floral scent bright, a heavier one gives a deeper, sweeter cup with caramel in it.

Mi Lan Xiang, honey orchid, is one of the traditional ten aroma types and one of the most widely made, often named as a good first Dancong. It is described as honey-sweet with an orchid scent, with a cooked sweet potato note, and a liquor from golden amber to orange-red, depending on the roast. The one name covers a range of teas.

Dancong means single bush: the leaf of one bush picked and made on its own, never mixed with others. The bushes are chosen from the old Phoenix Shuixian plants of the mountain. Today a named Dancong is mostly grown from cuttings or grafts of a chosen bush, so one name no longer means one tree, though some very old trees are still made on their own.

Old bushes, laocong, are prized for depth and a lasting sweetness, and give little leaf; no age is agreed for when a bush counts as old. Song variety, songzhong, is a market label for the oldest named lines, Huangzhi above all, not a proven age. A legend gives the old trees their name: the last Song emperor, fleeing as a boy, was given tea on the mountain by a phoenix.

Ya Shi Xiang, duck dung aroma, is the market name for a very floral Dancong, and most lists of the ten leave it out even though it sells widely. It is also called Yinhua Xiang, silver flower or honeysuckle aroma, a name put forward in 2014 for a scent likened to the wild honeysuckle of the mountain; many sellers keep the old name. Its line is traced to Pingkengtou village. Three stories explain the name, all told as stories: that it was chosen to put thieves off the bush, that it comes from the yellow local soil called duck dung soil, and that duck droppings lay on the bush. The tea tastes nothing like its name: every account of the cup gives flowers, usually with milk or cream, honey or fruit.

Dark tea is made to be kept, and the trade values it more with age. Over years it turns darker and redder in the cup and grows mellower and sweeter. How fast it changes depends on how it is stored, and the trade does not agree on one way: some keep it cool and dry for a slow, clean change, others warmer and more humid for a faster, deeper one. When a tea counts as young or aged differs from style to style, so each style sets its own measure.

Dark tea takes boiling water. Its leaf is mature and dense, so it gives up its flavour slowly and is hard to overbrew. Rinse it first with boiling water and pour that off within seconds: the rinse wakes the leaf and washes off dust and any stale smell from storage, and an old tea may take a second rinse. In a small pot use plenty of leaf, about 7 grams to 120 ml, then steep very briefly at first and a little longer each time; a good dark tea gives many cups.

From a brick, cake or basket, ease the leaf off along the edge or from the top with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole pieces give up their flavour steadily; crumbs release it all at once and cloud the cup.

Older or coarse dark tea is often simmered rather than steeped: the leaf goes into a pot of water, comes to a gentle boil and simmers for a few minutes. Thick leaf and long-aged tea release their flavour slowly, and the steady heat gives a fuller, smoother cup than short steeps do.

A smooth, mellow cup with low bitterness and a deep red colour, often sweet and woody or earthy, sometimes with herbal or medicinal notes. A young dark tea can still smell of the pile or of storage; an aged one is usually redder, sweeter and thicker.

Dark tea is Chinese tea whose leaf, after it is heated and rolled, is left to change in warmth and moisture, where microbes and the leaf’s own chemistry slowly darken and mellow it. Because that change comes after the leaf is made, the trade calls it post-fermented. In Chinese it is hei cha, “black tea”, which is not the English black tea; that tea is red tea, hong cha, in Chinese.

The first records of dark tea by name are from the Ming dynasty, in Hunan around Anhua and in Sichuan, and in the late Ming it became a state-managed tea sent to the north-west in exchange for horses. In the Qing dynasty merchants carried the craft to more regions and more shapes, and some styles were made for new markets: Guangxi’s Liu Bao, for one, went to the tin mines of Southeast Asia. In the twentieth century state factories took over much of the making and settled the brick shapes that are sold today.

Most dark tea shares four steps, each with a reason. The leaf is heated first, the kill-green, to stop its own enzymes from browning it; coarse leaf is often sprinkled with a little water so it heats evenly. It is rolled gently, because the large, mature leaf used for dark tea is tough and breaks if it is worked hard. It is then piled, and in the pile warmth, moisture and microbes do the darkening and mellowing, so the heap is turned to keep its heat in range. Finally it is dried, which stops the change and makes the tea stable enough to keep. Many styles then steam the leaf and press it, or pack it into baskets, and let it age.

Dark tea was made for people who lived far from where tea grows: Tibet, Mongolia, China’s north-west and, later, Central Asia and Russia. The trade called it border tea. The tea had to survive months on the road, so it was pressed into bricks, cakes and logs, or packed tight in baskets. A dense, even shape is easier to carry, stack and strap to a pack animal, and it keeps better than loose leaf. Some dark tea is still sold loose.
Dian Hong changes in storage, but the trade treats it as best in its first one to three years. It is kept for freshness rather than for age.
Dian Hong takes hot water, roughly 90 to 100°C. A common start is about 5 grams to 100 ml, with short steeps that lengthen slowly as the leaf opens.
A full, sweet cup, often described as malty, with chocolate or cocoa and honey notes and sometimes something floral. The liquor runs golden to bright red, and a good grade has little bitterness.

Dian Hong is red tea from Yunnan, made from the province’s large-leaf tea trees. Its home is Fengqing County in Lincang, in the south-west of the province, and it is also made in other parts of Lincang and in Menghai, Pu’er, Baoshan and Dehong. Golden buds through the dry leaf are the mark of the style.

When the war cut China off from its eastern tea regions, the country needed a new red tea to sell abroad, and the national tea company looked to Yunnan’s large leaf. Feng Shaoqiu reached Shunning, now Fengqing, in late 1938 and made a trial batch from one bud and two leaves. An experimental factory followed there in 1939, the start of today’s Fengqing factory. For decades nearly all Dian Hong went abroad; it was sold widely at home only from the 1980s.

Yunnan’s large-leaf trees give a plump leaf with many buds, and a strong cup. The trade ties that strength to the leaf’s high polyphenol content, which is also why Dian Hong stands up to milk. The buds turn golden as the tea is made, so a tea heavy in buds shows more gold.

Dian Hong follows the steps of every red tea: the leaf is withered, then rolled to break its cells so oxidation can begin, then left to oxidise until it turns from green to reddish brown, and then dried with heat, which fixes it and keeps the leaf golden. It is then sorted into grades. There are two broad kinds: gongfu, whole or strip leaf, and broken. The gongfu grades use one bud with one to three leaves, and teas of buds alone, sold as golden bud or golden needle, sit at the top. A grade name says nothing about where the leaf grew or how old the trees were.

Two newer branches sell under the Yunnan red name. Old-tree red is made from old tea trees; it is priced higher, and there is no agreed definition or standard for it. Sun-dried red is red tea whose last drying is done in the strong spring sun of the mountains rather than over heat, a choice of process and not a separate kind of tea. The trade does not agree whether either should be called Dian Hong.

The trade says white tea is tea in its first year, medicine at three years and a treasure at seven; it is a saying, not a tested claim, and no agreed number of years makes a tea aged. With age it moves from fresh and sweet toward jujube, dried fruit, honey, wood and herbs, with a deeper, redder liquor and a rounder body. Keep it dry, clean and aired, away from strong smells and sunlight.

Gongfu style, use about 1 gram of leaf to 15 to 25 ml of water, for example 5 grams in a 100 to 110 ml gaiwan; weigh it, since the leaf is light and bulky. Silver Needle and young, delicate tea take water below the boil, about 75 to 90°C; older, leafier or aged tea takes water at or near the boil. Start with a steep of 10 to 45 seconds and add a few seconds each round. An aged cake is often rinsed quickly first, and older pressed tea can be simmered on the stove, about 5 grams to 500 ml for 3 to 10 minutes; young, delicate tea is not.

Pressed white tea is new. Cakes began in the 2000s and spread around 2010, because a cake is smaller and easier to keep and carry than loose leaf. A cake is made from one of several grades, White Peony, Gong Mei or Shou Mei, so its grade has to be read from its own description. Some cakes are pressed from leaf already aged loose for a few years, so the year on a cake can be the year it was pressed rather than picked.
In young Fuding tea: a sweet cup, floral, fresh and brisk, with the scent of the down. Zhenghe tea is most often called thick and full.

Fuding grows two named cultivars, Fuding Da Bai and Fuding Da Hao, and Fuding Silver Needle is made from their buds; Fuding Da Bai comes from Bailiu village in Diantou and has plump buds heavy with white down. Zhenghe has its own, Zhenghe Da Bai, used for its Silver Needle and White Peony. Both replaced, mostly from the late 1800s on, the older small-leaf local plants grown from seed, called Cai Cha.

Fujian is the home of white tea. Fuding and Zhenghe are its two leading counties, and Jianyang and Songxi make white tea too. Fuding is a coastal city in the north-east of the province, by the Zhejiang border, hilly over most of its land; its white tea is tied to Taimu Mountain, where the first mother tree and the first famous bud tea are placed. Fuding white tea is a protected origin name in China. Zhenghe is an inland mountain county further west.

Fuding buds are plumper and downier than Zhenghe's. In the cup, Fuding is most often called the lighter, fresher, more floral style, and Zhenghe the fuller, thicker, mellower one. That is the trade's comparison of the two places, not a rule for every tea.

The trade sorts Fujian white tea by how the leaf was picked. Silver Needle is buds alone. White Peony is a bud with one or two young leaves. Gong Mei has more leaf than bud, and Shou Mei is the mature-leaf grade, with large leaves and few or no buds, often from later picks. Fuding also makes a separate new-craft white tea, xin gongyi, which is lightly rolled after withering and is darker in the cup.

White tea in its present form is a Qing dynasty tea of the 1700s and 1800s, first from Fuding or Jianyang and from Zhenghe later in the 1800s. Fuding Silver Needle was first sold abroad around 1890. The stories of Taimu and older uses of the name white tea are legend, kept apart from this record.

Two steps make it: withering, then drying at low heat, with no fixing and no rolling for the classic grades. The leaf is withered in the sun, indoors in moving air, indoors with gentle warmth, or by a mix of these, as the weather and the leaf allow, usually for two to three days. It is then dried at low heat, over charcoal or by machine, until it keeps.
Jujube or dried dates, herbs and medicine, wood, honey and dried fruit, a deeper, redder liquor, a thicker, rounder body, and less lift in the scent than a young tea.
In a cup or pot, steep it for about two to five minutes. It is forgiving of small changes in water temperature and steeping time. It can also be cold-brewed, steeped for some hours in the fridge.

Ripe, dried or stewed fruit such as apricot, honeyed sweetness, a smooth, round body, and little bitterness or astringency; often brown sugar or roasted grain, sometimes wood or spice, and a light fruity sourness.

GABA tea names a way of making tea, not a plant or a place. GABA, gamma-aminobutyric acid, is an amino acid found in tea leaf, and the leaf is treated so that the finished tea holds much more of it than ordinary tea. It can be made as green, oolong or red tea; oolong is the form Taiwan is best known for, where the tea research station named its version GABA oolong. In Japan, where the method began, it was called Gabaron, and in Taiwan the trade name is Jiayelong.

The method was found in Japan, by Dr Tsushida and colleagues at the government tea research institute, and the finding is dated to 1987. The first Japanese teas had a stuffy, sour smell and taste, and Taiwan's tea research station changed the method and adapted it to oolong. It spread among Taiwanese makers, and Taiwan is now a main source of GABA tea sold abroad. It needs no special leaf: ordinary oolong types serve.

The fresh leaf is held for some hours without oxygen, in a sealed chamber or drum filled with nitrogen or emptied to a vacuum. Without oxygen the leaf turns its glutamic acid into GABA and cannot break it down again, so it builds up. The leaf is then made in the usual way for its type; for oolong that means withering and tossing, fixing, rolling, drying and sometimes a roast. Taiwan's oolong method alternates rounds without oxygen and rounds in air, rather than one long hold.

The fresh leaf is kept for some hours without oxygen, in a sealed chamber or drum filled with nitrogen or emptied to a vacuum. Without oxygen the leaf turns its glutamic acid into GABA and cannot break it down again, so it builds up. The leaf is then made in the usual way for its type; for oolong that means withering and tossing, fixing, rolling, drying and sometimes a roast. Taiwan's oolong method alternates rounds without oxygen and rounds in air, rather than one long spell.

The figure most often given for calling a tea GABA tea is at least 150 mg of GABA in every 100 grams of dry tea. It is repeated widely for Japan and Taiwan, though no standard document behind it is quoted.

Greater Yiwu is often associated with a softer opening and a persistent sweet return when compared with the more forceful profiles linked to western Xishuangbanna. The area contains many growing places, however, and their material can vary substantially; this is a regional tendency, not a tasting promise for an individual tea.

Yiwu became an important collection and distribution point for tea from the old Six Famous Tea Mountains. Its trade connected local leaf, merchant networks, tribute routes, and later some of the best-known early twentieth-century tea firms.

Yiwu can mean a township, a market center, or a much broader tea area in eastern Xishuangbanna. In trade, the name often reaches beyond the town itself, so a Yiwu label should be read as a regional claim whose scale still needs context.

Green tea is a tea to drink fresh. The sources read give its best time as within about a year of picking, and a shelf life of a year or two when it is sealed. After that it goes flat: the fresh smell fades and the cup turns dull. Nothing read describes a tradition of ageing green tea, and it does not mature the way pu’er or white tea can. Keep it sealed, dark, dry and away from strong smells. If a green tea is sold as old, what counts is how it was kept, because the type itself does not promise anything.

Anhui is one of the main green tea provinces of China. Its best-known green tea is Huangshan Maofeng, from the Huangshan mountains: a slightly curled leaf covered in fine white down, fixed and then dried over gentle heat rather than in a pan, which is why it counts as oven-dried and not pan-fired.

Green tea takes water well below the boil, about 80°C, a little cooler for the youngest leaf and a little warmer for older, larger leaf. Boiling water draws out bitterness and dries the cup. A common start is about 2 grams of leaf to 100 ml, in a glass or a small gaiwan, with short steeps of half a minute to two minutes, and the same leaf can be brewed a few times.

A fresh, clean cup that many call crisp, with a sweet, soft finish, and a pale green to yellow-green liquor. The smell runs from fresh leaf to flowers, and steamed teas lean grassy or seaweed-like. Too much heat or too long a steep turns the cup bitter and drying.

Green tea is the tea whose leaf is never allowed to oxidise. Soon after picking, the leaf is heated, and the heat stops the leaf’s own enzymes before they can turn it brown, so it keeps its green colour and its fresh, leafy taste. That sets it apart from red tea, where the change is let run to the end, and from oolong, where it is stopped halfway. Green tea is made in many provinces of China, Zhejiang, Jiangsu and Anhui among them, and in Japan, Taiwan and elsewhere.

Green tea is made in three steps, and each has a reason. First the leaf is fixed, heated fast in a hot pan or drum, or with steam, to stop the enzymes; the Chinese trade calls this killing the green, and it is the step that makes the tea green. Then the leaf is rolled, twisted and pressed, so it takes its shape and lets out a little juice. Last it is dried, by pan, oven heat or sun, until only a few percent of water is left, so it keeps and does not go mouldy.

Green tea is sorted by how it is fixed and how it is dried. Pan-fired tea is dried in the pan and is the usual Chinese way; West Lake Longjing from Zhejiang, flat and straight, is the best-known example, and Biluochun from Jiangsu is curled into small snails. Steamed tea is fixed with steam, which is the usual Japanese way, and it gives a deeper green leaf and a grassier, sometimes seaweed-like taste. Oven-dried tea is dried over gentle heat after fixing, which leaves the leaf looser and keeps more of its white down. Sun-dried tea is dried in sunlight.

Lapsang has no recognised tradition of long ageing, and no category of decades-old red tea is described. Over its first few years in good storage the pine smoke softens and moves toward dried fruit, wood and sweetness. Keep it sealed, dry, cool and away from light and other smells; a smoky tea scents whatever is near it.

In a cup or pot, use about 3 grams for 240 ml, with water at 90 to 100°C, and steep about two to five minutes, usually around three. Gongfu style, use about 5 grams in a 100 to 110 ml gaiwan or pot, with short steeps that grow a little longer each round. Too hot or too long and the smoke turns harsh and bitter and covers the tea.
In the smoked tea: pine and pine resin, longan or dried longan, campfire or woodsmoke, dried fruit and a sweet aftertaste. In the unsmoked tea: honey, longan and fruit or flowers.

Zhengshan Xiaozhong is the red tea of Tongmu, in the Wuyi mountains of northern Fujian; its home villages and gardens lie inside the Wuyi mountains nature reserve. Zhengshan, true mountain, names the Tongmu core, and waishan, outer mountain, is tea made the same way outside it; how much that line says about quality is argued over. Lapsang Souchong is the Western name for it, taken from the Fuzhou dialect. In English the name now usually means the strongly smoked tea sold abroad, while in China Zhengshan Xiaozhong covers gentler and unsmoked tea too.

Zhengshan Xiaozhong is called the oldest red tea, the ancestor of red tea, born in Tongmu; the dates given for it differ. The usual story is of soldiers camped among the picked leaf in the harvest season: the leaf spoiled, the villagers dried it over pine fire, and the smoky tea was sold to Dutch buyers. The story is told, not recorded. The tea reached Europe first through Dutch and then British trade, under names such as Bohea and Souchong. In 2005 Tongmu makers devised Jin Jun Mei, a red tea of buds alone made the Lapsang way but not smoked, and it changed the village’s trade.

The leaf is withered, rolled and left to oxidise in covered baskets or cloth bags for some hours, until it turns reddish-brown to copper. It then goes into a hot pan, guo hong guo, which stops the oxidation fast, lifts the aroma and gives a sweeter, rounder cup, and is rolled again while hot, which shapes the strip and helps it take up smoke. In the traditional way the leaf is withered with pine heat in the qinglou and dried over the pine fire for most of a day.
The smoke softer and further back, with dried fruit coming forward.

The traditional tea is dried over a fire of local pine, and the pine smoke gives it its main aroma, with longan fruit said to sit in the same note. The work is done in a qinglou, a wooden house of several floors with the fire at the bottom and the leaf on bamboo mats above, so the heat and smoke rise through the leaf. The strongly smoked style was made for export and never took hold in China. An unsmoked Tongmu red tea now sits beside it, built up from about 2005 and made widely for the Chinese market. Cheap Lapsang from outside Tongmu is often flavoured or smoked by a shortcut rather than made in a qinglou.

Young single-origin Lincang sheng is often described as green, firm, and bitter. This reputation is useful as a starting point only: Lincang is a large prefecture, and material from its counties, mountains, and villages should not be collapsed into one tasting profile.

Lincang has a smaller public archive of famous aged single-origin teas than Yiwu or Menghai. Older blended productions, especially those associated with Xiaguan, nevertheless provide a historical thread, even when the exact origin of their base material cannot be reconstructed.

Lincang lies north of Pu’er Prefecture and against Myanmar to the west. Its tea geography includes Mengku, Yongde, Fengqing, Bangdong, Bingdao, and Xigui, with repeated place names such as Daxueshan making precise labels especially important.

Liu An is said to improve with years in its basket, turning mellower, rounder and redder in the cup. Young tea has an edge of charcoal or smoke that settles with age. Keep it dry, clean, away from smells and direct sun, in wrapping that breathes, not sealed airtight.

The tea is packed into woven bamboo baskets lined with bamboo leaf, from about 250 to 600 grams each, several tied into a bundle. The leaf lining gives the tea a bamboo note that sellers liken to rice dumplings, and drinkers keep the leaves to brew a small piece with the tea. Old baskets carry printed paper tickets naming the firm, which collectors use to tell editions and fakes apart. Sun Yi Shun is the best-known old firm, but modern baskets carry the name too, so the name alone does not date a basket.

Use water at or near the boil, rinse the leaf quickly, and keep the steeps short, each a little longer than the last, in a gaiwan or clay pot; doses run from about 3 to 8 grams for 100 ml, for six to ten or more steeps. A small piece of the basket's bamboo leaf is often brewed with it. Aged tea can also be simmered in a larger pot, about 1 gram to 200 to 300 ml, for a few minutes or longer.

Bamboo leaf above all, herbal or medicinal notes, a sweetness that returns after swallowing, a cooling feel in the mouth and throat, and a smooth, thick cup with little bitterness; young tea shows some smoke or charcoal, and the liquor runs from orange-gold to red.

Liu An basket tea is a dark tea packed into small bamboo baskets and kept for years. Despite its name it is made in Qimen County in southern Anhui, around Luxi and Rongkou, not in Lu'an, from the local small-leaf Qimen bush that Keemun red tea also comes from. In the south it was sold as Liu An, and sellers today use Liu An, Lu An, Lao Liu An and An tea for the same basket tea; the name is said to come from its following the Liu An way of making and trading. It is not Liu An Gua Pian, a green tea from the Lu'an area that only shares part of the name.

Spring leaf, picked around Grain Rain, is first made much like a green tea: withered, fixed, rolled and dried into rough tea, which rests through the summer. In early autumn it is sorted, graded, blended and fired over charcoal. Then comes the step most accounts single out: the fired tea is spread on bamboo mats outdoors for one night to take the dew, and gathered before sunrise. It is steamed soft, packed into baskets lined with bamboo leaf, tied into bundles and fired a last time over charcoal, and it is sold only after resting for some years, commonly three.
A redder, browner liquor, the smoke gone, and the cup moving toward medicinal, woody and camphor notes, often with betel nut.

Old baskets were kept in Hong Kong and Macau tea houses, medicine shops and homes, and the oldest are treated as collector's pieces, with prices that climb steeply with age. Fakes exist, so buyers look at the tickets, the basket's shape and the story of the stock.

Basket tea went south to Guangdong, Hong Kong, Macau and the overseas Chinese of Southeast Asia, and that is where it was known and drunk. It was kept in homes and medicine shops, added to herbal remedies, and older drinkers in the south still call it a cooling tea in the traditional Chinese sense. Production stopped in the 1930s and 1940s, as war cut the southern trade, and the tea was nearly gone for decades. In 1983 tea people from Hong Kong sent an aged basket to Anhui and asked for it to be made again, and commercial making returned in the early 1990s.

After about ten years the trade counts a Liu Bao as aged. The cup turns amber to deep red-brown, thick and smooth, with woody and herbal notes, and decades-old tea is often said to take on ginseng and camphor. How it was stored matters as much as how long, and the trade does not agree whether it keeps improving for decades or peaks sooner.
Between about five and ten years the aged character begins to show. The pile smell has gone, the cup deepens toward red, and the woody, sweet notes the trade looks for start to come through.
Under about five years a Liu Bao is still young. Its cup is paler, yellow to orange, and it can carry a faint smell of the pile and a little brightness or bitterness that age will soften.

Liu Bao takes very hot or boiling water, because its leaf is dense and gives up its depth slowly. Rinse it once or twice and pour the rinse away. Use about 5 to 8 grams to 100 ml, start with steeps of five to fifteen seconds and add a few seconds each round; a good Liu Bao gives ten cups or more.
A sweet, smooth cup, woody and herbal, which the trade sums up as red, thick, aged and mellow. The note most often named is betel nut, faint in younger tea and clearer with age.

Liu Bao is a dark tea from Cangwu County, near Wuzhou in Guangxi, named for the town of Liubao where it began. Like every dark tea, its leaf is piled after it is made, so that warmth, moisture and microbes turn it darker and softer, and then it is packed and left to age.

From the late 1930s war and blockade cut the river trade, and in the decades that followed production fell further as the planned economy changed who could buy and sell tea, and later as farmers left tea for other work. When the Malaysian tin mines declined, much old stock was left sitting in warehouses in Malaysia and Hong Kong. That forgotten stock is where most very old Liu Bao comes from today.

In the 1950s the Wuzhou tea factory worked out cold-water piling, around 1958: the leaf is wetted and heaped at a modest warmth and turned until it has darkened, a steadier route than the farmhouse steaming. Factory tea, too, is packed in baskets and aged before sale.

The older, farmhouse way of making Liu Bao leans on steam and time. The leaf is steamed to soften it, then heaped damp so it darkens and loses its bitterness, and in most accounts it is steamed again before it is pressed. It is dried slowly over a wood or pine fire, which can leave a faint smoke and keeps the leaf sound enough to age. Then it is packed tight into bamboo baskets and rested in a cool, damp, dark store for one to three years before it is sold.

Liu Bao was made for a market far from home. Chinese miners and labourers in Malaya and across Southeast Asia drank it, above all in the tin mines, and the trade held that it eased the heat and damp of their work and settled the stomach; it was also a taste of home. The tea went by boat down the river to Wuzhou, on to Guangzhou, and out by sea. In the Qing dynasty it was already counted among China’s famous teas.
