The tea went by boat down the river to Wuzhou, on to Guangzhou, and out by sea. In the Qing dynasty it was already counted among China’s famous teas.
A deep red, thick cup with woody, herbal and betel nut notes; tea several decades old is often described with ginseng and camphor.

Liu Bao that is several decades old is mostly stock that sat in Malaysia or Hong Kong after the mining trade ended. It is prized and hard to date, so the trade reads its age from the basket, the labels and the papers packed with it, and the place it was stored gives each lot its own character.

Mahei names the village in Yiwu. Gushu means “old tree,” the description on this tea’s label. Hong cha, the last two words, means “red tea.” Together the words give a place, a description of the trees and a style of tea.

A section of the old Tea Horse Road passes through Mahei. Ma Zhefeng photographed it while tracing the route through Yiwu. In April 2024, local reporters met Mahei farmer Ding Wanchun picking spring tea with his crew. He said his family needed more than twenty pickers a day.

Huiliu means “returned.” On a Malaysian Returned Liu Bao label, Malaysia names a stop in the life of the tea. Liu Bao made in Guangxi travelled overseas, and older tea later found buyers back in China.

A trade account published in 1951 follows Liu Bao downstream. At Libu the tea changed to a larger wooden boat for Fengkai, then to a powered vessel for Guangzhou. The account names Ipoh and Kuala Lumpur among its final markets.

On a visit to Wuzhou in 2024, Malaysian trade representative Lin Hengyi saw a 1973 import order linking a Malaysian firm and a Wuzhou tea company. His family still kept tea from the 1970s. During the visit, merchants asked him about bringing older Liu Bao back to the Chinese market.

Specialist writing often contrasts Menghai’s strength and bitterness with the gentler reputation of eastern Xishuangbanna. That comparison is a broad regional convention: tree material, craft, blend, age, and storage still create large differences within the county.

The establishment of Menghai Tea Factory and the post-1950 shift toward large-scale production made the county central to twentieth-century Pu’er. Regional leaf increasingly entered factory blends, connecting Menghai with many benchmark raw and ripe productions.
Naka is a village in Mengsong, one of Menghai County’s tea-growing areas.

Menghai County anchors much of western Xishuangbanna’s Pu’er landscape. Names such as Nannuo, Bulang, Mengsong, Hekai, Pasha, and Bada describe distinct mountain areas within the county rather than interchangeable synonyms for Menghai.

In the catalogue for a Malaysian tea fair in 2022, a dark rectangle of pressed tea sits among four cream wrappers printed in red. The exhibitor, Quanyuxuan, offered five Ruigong bricks together at stall 27. The caption identifies that particular offering as ripe tea from 2008, with 250 grams in each brick.

Nanqiao was once the name of the county around Mengzhe in southern Yunnan. Menghai County Nanqiao Tea Company, founded in February 2004, kept that old place name. The China Tea Marketing Association identifies Che Fo Nan as the company’s brand and records that it sold teas in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Southeast Asia.

Only well-made, well-roasted oolong is kept to age; the families most often aged are Wuyi rock tea, traditional Tieguanyin and roasted Taiwan oolong. Light, green-style oolong is a tea to drink fresh, and kept too long it goes flat or sour. Moisture is the danger: tea that was not dried and roasted enough takes up damp and turns grassy again. The heavier the roast, the more slowly the tea changes. Over years of storage good oolong is roasted again at low heat from time to time to drive off the moisture it has taken in, a skilled job that can cost some quality each round. Kept sealed, away from light, smells and damp, a roasted oolong softens with the years: the roast loses its edge, the body grows smoother and thicker, the liquor deepens towards red-brown, and the high floral aroma fades. There are no agreed ages at which oolong counts as aged.

Oolong is most often brewed gongfu style, in a small gaiwan or clay pot with plenty of leaf and short steeps, and it stands many rounds. A common start is about 4 to 6 grams to 100 ml, with a first steep of roughly 5 to 15 seconds and 5 to 10 seconds more each round. Light, green-style oolong takes water a little off the boil, about 90 to 95°C; heavily oxidised, roasted and aged oolong takes water at a full boil. Many people pour a quick first rinse to wake tightly rolled leaf. In a larger pot, use less leaf and steep for a few minutes.

In light, green-style oolong: floral and orchid notes, a creamy or buttery feel and a sweet aftertaste that lingers. In roasted and darker oolong: toasted grain and caramel, wood, stone fruit and a mineral, rock-like character.

Oolong is the partly oxidised tea, standing between green tea, which is not oxidised, and red tea, which is oxidised all the way. In Chinese it is also called qing cha, blue-green tea. The range inside it is wide: some oolongs sit close to green tea, floral and creamy, and others close to red tea, roasted, woody and dark-fruited. No single percentage describes the type, and the figures sellers give do not agree.

Oolong is made in four main families, each named for where it comes from and how it is made, not for quality. North Fujian makes Wuyi rock tea, strip-rolled, usually the most oxidised and most roasted, prized for a lasting mineral quality the trade calls rock rhyme. South Fujian, led by Anxi and its Tieguanyin, makes ball-rolled tea. The Phoenix mountain area of Chaozhou in Guangdong makes Dan Cong, strip-rolled and mostly named for its aroma, which comes from the bush and not from added flavour. Taiwan, whose tea came from Fujian, makes mostly light to medium oolong, usually ball-rolled, with high mountain tea the most popular style.

By the Qing dynasty oolong was an established craft in Fujian, refined in the Wuyi mountains and in Anxi during the 1700s, and the making of Tieguanyin in Anxi is dated to the early eighteenth century. The craft then spread to Chaozhou and to Taiwan, where oolong grew into an export tea in the second half of the nineteenth century. Where oolong first began, Wuyi or Anxi, is not settled, and the stories told about its name and its first makers are stories.

Oolong is made in a set order, and each step has a reason. The leaf is withered, often first in the sun and then indoors, so it goes soft enough to handle without breaking. It is then tossed or shaken in rounds with rests between them. The knocking bruises the leaf’s edges, which begin to oxidise, and the rests let the change spread slowly inward while the aroma builds. That is why a well-made oolong leaf is often green in the middle with a reddish edge. High heat, in a wok or a hot drum, then stops the change at the level the maker wants. The leaf is rolled, either into long twisted strips or, by rolling again and again in cloth, into tight balls. Last, it is dried, and many oolongs are then roasted.
A smooth, mellow and sweet cup, often with dried fruit or plum and wood, sometimes something herbal, little astringency, and an amber to red-brown liquor.

How far the leaf is oxidised and how hard it is roasted are two separate choices. Roasting, over charcoal in the traditional heavy styles and often in several rounds over days or weeks, lowers the moisture so the tea keeps, and it mellows the tea and adds depth. A tea can be lightly oxidised and barely roasted, as most modern Anxi Tieguanyin and Taiwan high mountain tea are, or lightly oxidised and roasted hard, as traditional Tieguanyin was. Wuyi teas are labelled light, medium or full roast for this reason.

Tea moved from Yunnan toward Tibet and farther markets along trading networks that are often grouped under the Tea Horse Road. That commerce supported mountain production, market towns, and enduring links between tea-growing communities and distant drinkers.

Pu’er belongs to Yunnan’s long tea history. The name now gathers a family of teas whose identity is tied not only to manufacture, but also to material, place, and the traditions that developed around them.

Modern Pu’er includes sheng and shou. Their processing paths differ, but both sit within a twentieth-century industry that restored tea gardens, expanded production, and developed distinct forms for domestic and export markets.
Red tea has no tradition of ageing. It is a tea to drink fresh: sealed, it keeps its quality for about a year and a half to three years, and after that it turns flatter.

Red tea takes water near the boil, about 90 to 100°C; hotter water draws out its aroma and flavour more fully, but its bitterness faster too. In a pot or mug, use about a rounded spoon of leaf for each cup and steep three to five minutes, less for broken leaf and a little less, and a little cooler, for a light, delicate tea. Left too long, it turns bitter and drying, because time and heat pull more tannins from the leaf.
A sweet cup, often with honey, floral or fruity notes, malt in many, and a brisk strength in the stronger teas. The liquor runs red, bright to deep.

Red tea is the tea English calls black tea. The Chinese name follows the colour of the brewed cup, which is red; the English one follows the dry leaf, which is dark. It is the fully oxidised tea: once the leaf’s cells are broken, its own enzymes work on it until it has turned from green to reddish brown. The Chinese trade calls that step fermentation.

By the trade’s own telling, red tea began in the Wuyi mountains of northern Fujian, around Tongmu, in the seventeenth century, though no record says exactly how or when it was first made. Dutch traders and then the British East India Company carried it to Europe under the names Bohea and Souchong. In the nineteenth century the craft spread to other Chinese provinces, among them Anhui, where Keemun began late in the Qing dynasty, and the British, having taken Chinese plants and tea makers to India, planted red tea in Assam and later Darjeeling. Taiwan’s red tea dates from the Japanese period, at Yuchi near Sun Moon Lake, and Yunnan’s Dian Hong from the late 1930s.

Red tea is made in four steps, each with a reason. The fresh leaf is withered, spread out until it loses water and goes soft enough to work. It is rolled, twisted and bruised so its juices and enzymes meet and the change can begin. It is left to oxidise in warmth and damp air, and the maker judges it by smell and colour, as the grassy smell turns floral or fruity and the leaf turns reddish brown. Then it is dried with hot air, which ends the change and makes the tea stable. Graded teas are then sorted and blended.

Red tea is made in two families. Whole-leaf strip tea, called gongfu in Chinese and orthodox in English, is rolled with care and is the choice for slow, attentive brewing. Broken-leaf tea, cut or crushed, gives its colour and strength fast, which is why it fills tea bags and suits milk tea.

In 2019 reporters stepped into Wuzhou Tea Factory’s brick-and-timber aging warehouse. Work on it began in 1953, the year the factory opened. Factory staff explained that the porous wooden boards help moderate moisture and temperature while the tea rests after fermentation.

Wuzhou Tea Factory uses handwoven bamboo baskets for its Three Cranes teas. The weave holds its shape and lets air pass through while the tea rests. The supply cooperative describes a network of village weavers, including older residents who earn an income making the baskets.

Wuzhou Tea Factory dates its cold-water piling method to 1958. Workers moisten the leaves and heap them for fermentation. Zhou Mingliang was among the first technicians to practise it. In 1963, Qin Jiquan joined the factory and learned it on shift. When He Meizhen joined the factory in 1988, Qin was one of the senior technicians who taught her.

In July 1959, Guangxi’s trade department circulated an account from tea makers in Buyi, in Cangwu County. Export buyers wanted a brighter, deeper red in the cup and a tighter twist to the leaf. The makers lowered the heat of the firing pan and rolled the leaves more firmly. The circular records how they changed their work in response to buyers overseas.

San He means “Three Cranes.” Wuzhou Tea Factory traces the birds on its trademark to Hegang Tower beside the factory. The works opened for the export trade in 1953. The factory registered the Three Cranes mark in October 1991, nearly four decades later.

Under about three to five years a raw pu’er is young. Its cup is pale, yellow-green to pale gold, fresh and lean, with a bite of bitterness and astringency that is meant to turn sweet in the throat. Some drink it young for that liveliness; others treat it as a tea to put away.

With years, a well-kept raw pu’er turns from pale gold toward amber and then red in the cup, and its bitterness and astringency soften as it grows smoother and sweeter. How fast depends on how it is pressed and stored. The trade does not agree where aged begins: some say ten years, many wait for twenty or more.

Sheng is not given shou’s rapid fermentation. Its character instead changes gradually during storage, with leaf, liquor, aroma, and texture developing over years. Storage conditions therefore belong to the tea’s history, not as a guarantee of quality but as part of how any particular cake has evolved.

Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.
Pry the leaf off a cake or brick in chunks with a pick or knife, from the surface and toward the centre, rather than crumbling it. A mix of larger pieces and smaller ones brews evenly.

In young raw pu’er, a bitter, drying bite that turns into a returning sweetness, a feel in the throat that makes the mouth water, and fresh, floral or fruity notes such as apricot or plum. Tea kept in humid storage can carry a damp, earthy storage taste.

In the Qing dynasty pu’er went to the court as tribute, but far more was ordinary trade, carried as pressed tea along the Tea Horse Road to Tibet and Southeast Asia. In the twentieth century Hong Kong became its great drinking market, and merchants there kept it in humid stores to speed its change. After 1949 the private tea houses were folded into state factories, among them Menghai, Xiaguan and Kunming, which made pu’er to standard recipes under the state tea company’s labels.

Through the 1980s and 1990s collectors, led at first by Taiwan, came looking for aged raw pu’er, and demand grew into a speculative boom in which fakes and falsely aged tea were common. Since that boom buyers have turned from factory brands to named mountains, villages and old trees, and prices for famous origins have risen.
Sheng is the undarkened branch of Pu’er, often called raw Pu’er in English. The label distinguishes it from shou, whose accelerated post-fermentation creates a markedly different tea from the outset.

Raw pu’er begins as leaf from Yunnan’s large-leaf tea trees. It is picked and withered, then fried in a wok to kill the green. That heat stops most of the leaf’s own enzymes but not all, and because the leaf is never hot-air dried afterwards, the activity that survives is what lets the tea keep changing for years. It is rolled, then dried in the sun, turned over a couple of days. The result is maocha, the rough tea that is sold loose or pressed.
A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.

Maocha is pressed into cakes, bricks and tuo, small bowl shapes, either under a stone or by a hydraulic press; a stone-pressed cake is looser than a machine-pressed one. Pressing began so the tea could travel: compact cakes packed well onto pack animals on the old trade routes. It also decides how a tea ages, because a tight, large cake changes slowly and a loose or small one faster.

Maocha names an intermediate state in tea production, while sheng describes the tea as it reaches the drinker. Sheng material may be sorted, dried, left loose, or steamed and compressed; the two terms overlap, but they describe the tea from different viewpoints.

Raw pu’er ages partly through slow oxidation and partly through the work of microbes, so heat and humidity decide how fast it changes. Humid, warm stores, the traditional storage of Hong Kong and Guangdong, change it quickly; dry, cool stores, with Kunming as the usual example, change it slowly and keep it brighter, and a store that is too dry can leave a tea stalled and green. The trade does not agree whether humid storage is a flaw or a style of its own. At home, keep a cake wrapped in paper, away from smells and direct sun, at roughly 60 to 75 percent humidity.

After ten years or more, a well-kept ripe pu’er grows smooth and deep, with woody, date-like or medicinal notes the trade calls aged aroma. The leaf keeps changing slowly with the air and moisture around it, which is why storage matters as much as age: dry, clean storage keeps it bright, and damp storage leaves it musty.
Between about five and ten years the pile note has usually aired away. With it gone, the cup turns cleaner and rounder, and its sweetness comes forward.

In its first few years a ripe pu’er often still carries the smell of the pile, a damp, earthy note left over from fermentation that the trade calls pile taste. Air carries it off, so it fades with airing and with time, and a rinse or two before drinking helps.

Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.
From a cake, brick or tuo, ease a piece off along the edge with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole leaves give up their flavour steadily; broken ones release it all at once and cloud the cup.
A smooth, sweet cup with earthy or woody notes. A young ripe tea can carry a faint smell of the pile, which fades with airing or in the first steeps.

Ripe pu’er is pu’er whose leaf is fermented in a warm, damp pile before it is pressed or sold loose. The pile was developed to give, in weeks, the dark and mellow cup that Hong Kong and Guangdong drinkers knew from raw pu’er aged for years. So ripe pu’er is ready to drink soon after it is made, while raw pu’er skips the pile and is usually aged for years.
A smooth, deep cup with woody, date-like or medicinal notes, which the trade calls aged aroma.

In 1973 a team of seven from the Kunming, Menghai and Xiaguan factories went to the Guangzhou tea factory to learn its wet piling. Guangzhou piled with warm water. In Kunming’s cooler, drier air that failed, and Kunming succeeded in 1974 with cold water, sending about ten tonnes to Hong Kong that year. Menghai and Xiaguan each worked out their own ways, and by 1975 Menghai’s method had settled into the ripe pu’er made today.

Before 1949, pu’er already reached Hong Kong and Guangzhou red in the cup. Leaf was packed damp into bamboo baskets, the caravan journey could take a year, and merchants kept the tea for years more before selling it. When faster transport brought fresher tea in the 1950s, those drinkers missed the old taste, and the trade set out to hurry it. In Macau and Hong Kong, Lu Zhuxun sprinkled leaf with water to speed its change. From 1959 the Guangdong tea company in Guangzhou developed a faster fermentation, often blending Yunnan leaf with Guangdong leaf. Yunnan had its own beginnings too: dampening leaf for its pressed jin cha, and in 1958 a steam method at Xiaguan that cut fermentation to about fifteen days.

Most traditional factories still pile on cement floors or in tiled pits, seasoned over years of use; a new floor is first broken in with wetted tea dust until it darkens and stops smelling. Some newer makers pile off the floor on perforated steel to keep the leaf cleaner. A pile can be a hundred kilograms or twenty tonnes, and each maker decides how far to take it: a lighter fermentation keeps some of the raw leaf’s liveliness, a heavier one gives a thicker, darker cup, and taken too far the leaf turns hard and charred.
Ripe pu’er is made by fermenting tea leaves in a damp pile, a process called wet piling.

Ripe pu’er is made by fermenting tea leaves in a damp pile, a process called wet piling. Sun-dried leaf is wetted and heaped so that heat, moisture and microbes can work on it. The heat comes from the microbes themselves, so the pile is covered to hold it in, then turned about once a week to spread it and let air in. It is kept below about 65°C, because hotter than that the leaf starts to char. After one to two months the leaf is dried. Yunnan’s state factories brought the method into production in 1973, after a joint team studied faster piling in Guangdong.

Sichuan border tea is kept for years, and the trade values older bricks more. With age the liquor turns redder and the cup grows milder and rounder, and a medicinal edge often appears, which sellers read as a sign of good storage. Keep the brick dry, clean and away from strong smells and direct sun. Do not drink a brick that smells musty or shows mould. How fast it changes depends on storage, and the trade does not agree on one best way to keep it.

Break a few pieces from the edge of the brick, rinse them with boiling water and pour that off at once. Then use boiling water and plenty of leaf. The leaf is coarse and gives up its flavour slowly, so people brew it two ways. Some steep it in short gongfu pours, a little longer each time. Others use long steeps while the pot is still hot, or simmer the leaf for several minutes in a pot, which is the traditional way on the plateau.

In Tibet the brick is broken up and boiled for a long time, often for hours, until the liquor is very dark. The tea is strained and kept as a concentrate. A little is poured into a tall wooden churn with yak butter and salt and churned until the three are blended. It is served hot, in many bowls a day, and offered to every guest. Sichuan border tea has long been sent to Tibet for this.
A smooth, mellow cup with a red to dark brown liquor and a gentle sweetness, often with wood or earth.

Sichuan border tea is a dark tea made around Ya'an in western Sichuan and pressed into dense bricks for the Tibetan highlands. The trade has called it southern-route border tea, border-sale tea and, today, Ya'an Tibetan tea. It is made from mature leaf and red moss, the reddish stem and shoot pieces that come with the leaf, not from young buds. Coarse leaf was the choice for a tea that had to survive months on the road and then be boiled for hours. Two brick styles are sold today, Kangzhuan and Jinjian.

Kangzhuan and Jinjian are the two bricks sold today, and some Chinese pages list a third, Kangjian. Both use mature leaf and red moss, and the usual way to tell them apart is the blend. Kangzhuan carries more leaf, and Jinjian carries more red moss and stem. The two names are for the blend, so they say nothing by themselves about where a brick was made or how old it is.

The making has two stages. First comes rough tea. The mature leaf is heated to stop its own enzymes, then steamed, rolled and piled in repeated rounds, so that warmth, moisture and microbes darken and mellow it. Accounts count the steps differently, from about 18 to more than 30. Then comes the brick. The rough tea is sorted and blended for the style, steamed, pressed and dried, and rested in a pile so that it keeps changing around the pressing. Accounts differ on whether the rest comes before or after the press. The steam softens the coarse leaf so that it holds together as a brick, and the blend is how the maker sets how much leaf and how much red moss go in.
A redder, browner liquor, a rounder body and a medicinal edge, often with wood and a dark sweetness.

The bricks did not travel loose. They were bound into long packs of woven bamboo strips, called strip packs, and several were tied together for the road. At Kangding, tea going far into Tibet was sewn into yak hide. The hide was soaked, sewn around the load and hardened as it dried, which kept the tea dry and tight on a long journey.

Tea from Ya'an went west for about a thousand years. Under the Tang and Song dynasties it was traded for Tibetan horses, and in the Song the state set up offices to run that trade. The Sichuan road ran from Ya'an to Kangding and on to Lhasa. Porters carried the bricks on their backs from Ya'an to Kangding, a walk of more than ten days, because the mountain track was too steep for loaded horses. At Kangding the tea was repacked and went on by mule and yak. Tibetans needed it every day, in a cold land where the diet is meat, butter and barley. Porters gave way to trucks in the middle of the twentieth century, when the highway to Tibet opened.

Taiwan has a tradition of keeping oolong for years, called lao cha, old tea. The tea chosen for keeping starts well roasted and dry, and it is roasted again at low heat from time to time to drive out the moisture it takes in; how often is a matter of the keeper’s judgement. Stored cool, dry, dark and sealed, it loses its bitterness and astringency with the years, the cup turns smooth, round and sweet, and the liquor deepens through amber towards red-brown. No standard says how many years make an oolong old; those who give a figure put it somewhere between ten and thirty years.

Baozhong is made in the north of Taiwan, mostly in Pinglin and the nearby Wenshan area, and is the most lightly oxidised Taiwan oolong. Unlike most Taiwan oolong it is left as a long twisted strip, not rolled into balls, and it is normally dried rather than roasted. The name means wrapped kind, from the old habit of wrapping the tea in paper.

Ball-rolled Taiwan oolong takes hot water, about 90 to 100°C, a fairly generous amount of leaf and short steeps; the balls open slowly and give many infusions. Roasted Dong Ding takes water from about 95°C to a full boil. Aged oolong takes very hot water, in a pot that holds its heat, clay above all. Oriental Beauty is the exception and takes cooler water, about 80 to 95°C.

In light high mountain tea: a sweet, floral cup, often creamy or buttery, with little bitterness and a long sweet aftertaste. In roasted Dong Ding: caramel, ripe fruit, nuts and a toasted aroma. In Baozhong: floral notes and a clear, bright liquor. In Oriental Beauty: ripe fruit and honey, with little bitterness.

Taiwan oolong is the oolong of Taiwan, whose tea plants and craft came from Fujian. Most of it is lightly to moderately oxidised and rolled into balls, and Qingxin oolong is the main cultivar, with Jinxuan the other common one. The island makes several distinct styles: high mountain tea, Dong Ding from Lugu in Nantou, Baozhong from the north, and Oriental Beauty from Hsinchu and Miaoli.

Dong Ding oolong comes from Lugu Township in Nantou County, and its name is also used for the style made elsewhere. The leaf is withered in the sun and indoors with tossing, fixed, rolled into balls in cloth, dried, and then roasted. Traditional Dong Ding is roasted over charcoal, longan wood among the fuels; electric roasters are used too. It grows near or below the high mountain line, so it is not counted as high mountain tea.

High mountain tea, gao shan cha, is tea from gardens at about 1,000 metres and higher. It is a label for where the tea grew, not a cultivar or a recipe. The best-known areas are Alishan in Chiayi, Lishan in Taichung, Shanlinxi and Yushan, and Dayuling. At altitude the leaf grows slowly and comes out thick and fleshy, and the trade explains its sweetness and low bitterness by that slow growth. The usual high mountain tea is lightly oxidised, rolled into balls and left unroasted or only lightly roasted.

Oolong came to Taiwan with settlers from Fujian and was grown for sale in the nineteenth century. In the 1860s the Scottish merchant John Dodd, working with the Taipei merchant Li Chunsheng, sold it abroad as Formosa Oolong, and tea became one of the island’s leading exports, which it stayed under Japanese rule. In the late twentieth century the market turned inward: more Taiwan tea was drunk at home than sold abroad, and high mountain oolong became one of the island’s most prized teas.

Muzha, in southern Taipei, is the home of Taiwan’s traditional Tieguanyin. The tea master Zhang Naimiao is credited with bringing the cultivar there from Anxi, with a clansman, during the years of Japanese rule in Taiwan; the year is told differently. The traditional Muzha style is a more oxidised, charcoal-roasted tea, its leaf wrapped in cloth and rolled again and again.
A smooth, mellow, thick cup with little astringency, often plum or prune, sometimes something like medicinal herbs or ginseng, and an amber to red-brown liquor.

Oriental Beauty is made from buds and leaves bitten by a small green leafhopper. The bite starts the leaf’s change on the bush and is the root of the tea’s character, which is why its growers avoid insecticide on those fields. It is picked in early summer, is far more oxidised than other Taiwan oolong, close to red tea, and comes mainly from Hsinchu County, around Beipu and Emei, and from Miaoli. Its older name is Pengfeng tea, bragging tea.

Light, low-roast Tieguanyin is for drinking fresh and goes stale fast; the heavier charcoal-roasted kind is steadier and is the kind kept for years. Freshly roasted tea tastes of fire and is rested, months or years, until the fire settles. With age the tea softens: the fire fades, the liquor deepens, the body grows rounder and smoother and less sharp, and well-aged roasted tea often shows a soft fruity sourness. Keep it sealed, dry, dark and cool, away from strong smells, and look at it now and then; roasted tea does not need the refrigerator, which is for the light style.

Tieguanyin is usually brewed gongfu style with water at or near the boil, about 95 to 100°C; the light green style is often taken a little cooler, about 85 to 95°C. Use about 4 to 8 grams of leaf in a 100 to 150 ml gaiwan or pot, about a third full. A quick rinse, poured off at once, is common. Steeps start short, about 10 to 30 seconds, and grow a few seconds longer each round, and a good Tieguanyin gives about six to eight. In a larger pot, use about 2.5 to 5 grams for 240 to 350 ml and steep two to three minutes.

In the light style: orchid and other flowers, a fresh, clean cup and a sweet aftertaste. In the roasted style: toast and charcoal, caramel or honey, stone or dried fruit, nuts, and a liquor that runs from gold to amber.

Tieguanyin is the name of a tea cultivar and of the oolong made from it. The tea comes from Anxi County in southern Fujian, where the name is protected as Anxi Tieguanyin, and the trade names Xiping township in Anxi as the place it began; Gande is another of the best-known Anxi townships. The name joins iron and Guanyin, the bodhisattva of mercy. The finished leaf is usually rolled into tight balls that open slowly in the cup. Outside Anxi, in Taiwan above all, the name can mean a way of making the tea rather than the plant.

Anxi Tieguanyin has a national standard, GB 19598, first in force in 2005 and since replaced by a 2025 version. Brands print grade words such as tèjí, special grade, and yījí, first grade, in their names and listings.

The quality the trade prizes in good Tieguanyin is called Guanyin rhyme, guanyin yun. It is a tasting word for the whole effect: an orchid or floral fragrance, a thick, sweet taste, and an aftertaste and throat feeling that lingers. Good Tieguanyin is said to stay fragrant after seven infusions, a trade saying rather than a tested limit.

Two stories are told of how Tieguanyin began, both set in Xiping and both folk accounts, not records. In one, a farmer named Wei dreams of Guanyin, is led to a tea plant and grows it, in the Yongzheng reign of the 1720s and 1730s. In the other, a scholar named Wang finds a tea plant and presents its tea to the Qianlong emperor, who names it. Anxi sources date the making of oolong in Anxi to about 1725 to 1735.

The leaf is picked when the shoot has opened, withered in the late-afternoon sun, cooled, then shaken and rested in rounds. Shaking bruises the leaf edges so they turn red while the middle stays green, the green leaf with a red rim. The leaf is fixed in a hot pan or drum and rolled. To make the balls, it is wrapped in cloth, rolled and pressed, dried a little, and wrapped again, several times over, each round tightening it. It is finished with a slow drying at low heat.
A smoother, rounder, softer cup with the fire gone, a liquor turned orange-red or reddish-brown, and often a soft fruity sourness.
Osmanthus Tieguanyin is a scented tea. Fresh osmanthus flowers are layered with the finished tea, which takes up their scent, and the tea is then dried again.

Anxi Tieguanyin is sorted by style. The light-fragrance kind, qingxiang, is lightly oxidised and lightly roasted or not roasted at all, with a fresh orchid fragrance and a green-gold liquor. The strong-fragrance kind, nongxiang, is more oxidised and roasted, with a darker leaf, a gold to amber liquor and toasted, caramel and fruit notes. A third kind, chenxiang or old Tie, is Tieguanyin kept for years. The roasted style is the older one; the light green style is newer and took over in Anxi from the 1990s, and the roasted style is said to be slowly coming back.

Well-made, dry white tea is kept to age, and the trade speaks of new white tea and old white tea, lao bai cha. Over the years it changes rather than going stale: the fresh hay and floral notes give way to honey, dried fruit, jujube, herbs and wood, the liquor turns deeper and redder, and the body rounder and thicker. There is no agreed number of years at which white tea counts as aged. Keep it dry, sealed and away from light, damp and strong smells.

The more delicate the leaf, the cooler the water. Silver Needle and young White Peony take water well below the boil, roughly 75 to 95°C; Shou Mei and aged white tea take water near or at the boil. In a gaiwan or small pot, about 3 to 7 grams to 100 to 150 ml, with short steeps that lengthen each round. White tea is light and bulky, so weigh it rather than measure by the spoon.

In young white tea: a sweet, light cup, often floral, with hay and a honeyed finish. Silver Needle is the softest, with hay and gentle flowers; White Peony is fuller; Gong Mei and Shou Mei are stronger and rounder, with dried fruit and herbs.

White tea is the tea made with the fewest steps: the leaf is only withered and dried. It is never heated to stop its change, never rolled and never bruised, so the leaf keeps its natural shape and the white down on its buds stays, which gives the tea its name. It oxidises only lightly and slowly as it withers, by the leaf’s own enzymes; the Chinese trade calls it slightly fermented. White tea is made mainly in Fujian, and other regions, Yunnan among them, now make it too.

The two main homes of white tea are Fuding and Zhenghe, both in Fujian, and each grows its own cultivar: Fuding Da Bai, with large, plump, downy buds, and Zhenghe Da Bai, a taller bush with smaller buds. Fuding is the home of Silver Needle and of the best-known white tea; Zhenghe, further inland, is described as making a fuller tea. Jianyang is a white tea county too, known mostly for Gong Mei and Shou Mei.

White tea is sold by how the leaf was picked. Silver Needle, the top grade and picked in spring, is buds alone. White Peony is a bud with one or two leaves. Gong Mei and Shou Mei are larger, more mature leaf, often picked later in the year, and are the usual leaf for pressed cakes. A grade name says how the leaf was picked; it says nothing about where it grew.

White tea in its present form is a Fujian tea of roughly the last two centuries, from the late Qing dynasty. Older Chinese writings use the name white tea for other teas, and the exact year and place of the first white tea are not settled.

Withering is the step that makes white tea. The leaf is spread out and left to lose its water slowly, over roughly one to three days, and in that time small changes soften its grassy edge and shape its aroma and taste. It can be withered in the sun, indoors in moving air, or indoors with gentle warmth, and many makers combine them, choosing by the weather. Too short a wither leaves the tea grassy and bitter; too long leaves it thin and dull, and the maker judges by the leaf’s softness and smell. The leaf is then dried at low heat until it keeps, and sorted.
Honey, dried fruit or jujube, something herbal and woody, a rounder, thicker body and a darker, redder liquor, with less lift in the aroma than a young tea.

White tea was sold loose until recently. Pressed cakes appeared in the 2000s and became common in the 2010s, mostly made from Shou Mei and Gong Mei, because a cake is easier to keep. Pressed and kept, white tea moves from light and floral towards something deeper and sweeter.

Designer Yin Huize recalled taking hand-painted cartons to the spring Canton Fair with his colleague Tang Zheng. Buyers placed orders from the samples. Tang drew on an openwork jade tiger pendant for the Jixing mark. Yin framed the lettering on the black box with patterns inspired by Chinese lacquerware. The design later appeared on a miniature 15 g carton that airlines gave to passengers.

Much of Yunnan’s loose pu’er once travelled in bulk. In Japan, importers repacked it under their own labels. In 1980, Yunnan brought packaging and tea export designers together so a box could reach a shop counter carrying the province’s own brand. Y562 had Chinese lettering on the front and the English name “Superior Yunnan Pu-erh Tea” on the back. Its companion in the range was Y671, the “little yellow box.”

Y562 is the export code for a loose ripe pu’er from Yunnan. Drinkers nicknamed it the “little black box” after its carton. The Jixing brand mark on the front shows a tiger coming downhill. China Tea’s catalogue lists Y562 in the classic 100 g format.

Pu’er magazine describes the original Y562 blend as grades five and six of ripe tea supplied by Menghai Tea Factory. Its yellow-box companion, Y671, used grades six and seven supplied by Kunming Tea Factory. These grades describe how the leaf was sorted for the original blends.

Well-made medium to full roast Wuyi tea is the kind kept for years; light roast is for early drinking and is the most likely to go green again, a raw, sour or muddy taste that comes from damp or under-dried tea and is the main fault of stored rock tea. The heavier the roast, the longer the tea is said to stay good. With age the sharp roast softens, the liquor grows thicker and smoother and the high aroma fades. A tea that has gone green can be roasted again at low heat to drive out the moisture, a skilled job that costs some quality each time. Keep it sealed, dry, cool and away from strong smells, and look at it now and then.

Wuyi tea is usually brewed gongfu style with water at or near the boil, about 95 to 100°C, and about 5 to 8 grams of leaf in a 100 to 120 ml gaiwan, a third to a half full. A quick rinse, poured off at once, is common. Steeps start short, about 5 to 20 seconds, and grow a few seconds longer each round, and good rock tea gives seven steeps or more. In a larger pot, use about 2 to 5 grams for 250 to 350 ml and steep two to three minutes.

Roast and stone fruit, a mineral, rocky texture and a long, sweet, mouth-watering finish. Light roast is bright and floral, medium roast fruity and rounded, full roast charcoal, wood and roasted nuts. Da Hong Pao is often floral, Rougui spicy with cinnamon, young Shui Xian sweet and smooth, and old-bush Shui Xian woody and mossy.

Da Hong Pao, Big Red Robe, began with six old bushes on a cliff at Jiulongke in Wuyi, the mother trees, and picking from them stopped in 2006. Three kinds of tea are sold under the name: tea from the mother trees, which is extremely scarce, so any such claim deserves doubt; purebred tea from Qidan, the cultivar grown from cuttings of the mother trees; and commercial Da Hong Pao, which is most of what is sold and is usually a blend of several Wuyi cultivars. The name is also used loosely for other Wuyi teas.

Wuyi rock tea, yan cha, is the oolong of the Wuyi mountains around Wuyishan City in northern Fujian, and only tea from that area may be sold under the name. The bushes grow among rock, in crevices, on ledges and on terraces in cliff country, in soil weathered from the rock, with much fog and rain. The leaf is twisted into long thin strips, not rolled into balls, and it is finished with a long charcoal roast.

The trade sorts Wuyi tea by where it grew. Zheng yan, true rock, is the core rocky area and the most prized, its best-known part called the three pits and two streams. Ban yan, half rock, is the ring of edges and foothills around it, whose tea has some rock rhyme but less, and is often the better value. Zhou cha is tea from the river banks and flat land, not from rock.

Northern Fujian made tribute tea for the court in the Song dynasty. Early in the Ming dynasty the emperor ended the tribute of pressed tea cakes in favour of loose leaf, and tea making in the region turned to loose leaf. Oolong, partly oxidised tea, took shape in the Wuyi area between the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, around the end of the Ming and the start of the Qing.

Wuyi tea follows the oolong steps: it is withered in the sun and then cooled indoors, shaken and rested, fixed in a hot pan or drum, rolled into strips and given a first drying. Much of it is now made with machines guided by hand judgement, and fully hand-made tea is rare. What sets it apart is the roast: over charcoal, in several rounds with rests of weeks or months between them, not in one pass. The roast dries the tea so it keeps, and it takes away the raw, grassy taste, deepens the tea and adds fruit and a charcoal fragrance. The roast is matched to the leaf: thick, mature leaf takes a stronger roast, thin and aromatic leaf a lighter one.
Meizhan is a Fujian cultivar that came from Anxi, and it is also made as Wuyi rock tea. It is less famous than Rougui and Shui Xian and is not one of the four famous bushes of Wuyi.
A smoother, thicker liquor with less sharpness, the roast softened and the high aroma faded.

Wuyi tea is labelled by its roast. Light roast keeps bright floral notes and is for drinking early. Medium roast is the balanced middle, floral and fruity together. Full roast shows the clearest charcoal and fire notes and keeps the longest. A freshly roasted tea is rested so the fire note settles, and the heavier the roast, the longer the rest.

The quality the trade prizes in Wuyi tea is called rock rhyme, yan yun. It is described as something felt in the mouth as much as tasted: aroma, taste and body together, with a lasting sweet, mouth-watering aftertaste, and it is tied to the rocky ground the tea grows in. The Chinese phrase paired with it is yan gu hua xiang, rock bone and floral fragrance.
Rougui, cassia, is a Wuyi cultivar named for the cinnamon-bark smell of its finished tea. It dates from the Qing dynasty and is now one of the most widely planted and best-selling Wuyi teas.

Shui Xian is the most widely grown and drunk Wuyi cultivar and usually the least expensive of the main teas. It came to Wuyi in the Qing dynasty from elsewhere in northern Fujian, and Wuyi Shui Xian is traditionally roasted a shade darker than most rock tea. Lao cong, old-bush Shui Xian, comes from older bushes, costs more and is said to carry a woody, mossy character of its own, and Shui Xian, old bush above all, is the Wuyi tea most often said to age well.

Yunnan white is pressed and kept like Fujian white, and some keep it for years, but there is no agreed view of how long it should be kept or how it compares with aged Fujian white; some say it is best within a few years.
Yunnan white is brewed gently, as a white tea is, in a gaiwan or small pot, and it gives many infusions; the leaf holds up well.

A honeyed, sweet cup, often richer and fuller than Fujian white, with little bitterness, sometimes fruit like apricot or melon and a hay or herbal note. Yabao is sweet and silky, often with pine or herbal notes.

Yunnan white is white tea made from Yunnan’s large-leaf tea plants, rather than from the small and medium-leaf bush cultivars of Fujian. It is mostly picked in spring, as buds or a bud with one to three leaves, and its buds are typically large and silver-haired. Unlike Fuding white tea it is mostly not sold by grade.
Yunnan white is a recent tea in the market. The name Moonlight White and the trade in Yunnan white tea have grown popular only in recent years, though local practice may be older.

Yunnan white follows the white tea way: the leaf is withered and then dried, never heated to stop its change and never rolled. The withering is done indoors or in shade rather than in hot midday sun, and the leaf is then dried by air, without the final low bake that Fujian white tea usually gets. A longer or darker wither gives a darker, redder cup. It is sold loose and pressed, in the cake, coin and brick shapes of pu’er.

Moonlight White, yue guang bai, is the best-known Yunnan white. Its home is Jinggu County in Pu’er City, and the Jinggu tea is made from the Jinggu Da Bai Cha variety, whose mother tree grows in Yangta village; other Yunnan makers use the name too. Two explanations are given for the name: the look of the leaf, dark on top and silver beneath, like the moon in a dark sky, and a story that it was picked or withered by moonlight.

Yabao is made from the buds of wild-growing or old trees in south-west Yunnan, picked in late winter or early spring before they open and sun-dried with little else done to them. It is mostly sold as white tea. Which plant the buds come from is not settled: some are said to be from a wild tea species, not the cultivated tea plant.
Pu’er is unusually place-bound for a broad tea family. Yunnan is the central geographic frame, while comparable processing outside the province does not by itself make a tea Yunnan Pu’er.

Regional schemes are editorial aids rather than a single settled ladder. Boundaries, spellings, and the prominence given to one place over another vary, and famous names also function as commercial language. A place label is useful context, not proof of a tea’s exact origin.

Reference maps commonly begin with Xishuangbanna, Pu’er Prefecture, and Lincang, then move toward counties, mountain areas, villages, and local names. Xishuangbanna is often divided into eastern and western tea areas, while other production extends through Yunnan beyond those best-known centers.
